bibliographic.title: Governed AI-Assisted Engineering: Graduated Human Oversight for Agentic Code Generation in Regulated Domains
bibliographic.citation_apa: Kang, R. (2025). Governed AI-Assisted Engineering: Graduated Human Oversight for Agentic Code Generation in Regulated Domains. Preprint.

methodology.method_family: conceptual framework development with regulatory mapping, comparative framework analysis, and analytical productivity modeling
methodology.study_design: three-tier graduated oversight framework (GAIE) with Oversight Classification Model (OCM); evaluation via regulatory coverage analysis, comparative framework analysis, and analytical productivity modeling
methodology.sector: banking, insurance, healthcare, energy, financial services
methodology.technology_context: agentic AI coding systems; multi-agent supervisor architecture with human interaction layer, evidence capture, and monitoring; references OWASP LLM Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS

eligibility.decision_rationale: The paper strongly addresses graduated human oversight, compliance evidence, audit trails, and regulated-domain governance for agentic LLM-based systems, but its primary focus is software engineering and agentic code generation rather than conversational AI governance, chatbots, or customer-facing conversational systems central to the review scope.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Conversational AI relevance is indirect (IDE copilots, human interaction layer); confirm whether agentic coding governance counts within the review's conversational-governance inclusion criteria.

appraisal.notes: Clear framework contribution with mapped regulatory references and stated evaluation methods, but provided text shows no empirical field sample or primary data collection; productivity estimates (84–97%) derive from analytical modeling rather than observed deployment studies.

cerqual.explanation: Internally coherent governance framework with explicit oversight tiers and compliance artifacts, but evidence in the provided text is primarily conceptual and analytical rather than empirically validated; relevance to conversational-governance scope is partial because the dominant context is agentic code generation.

coding.theme: Governance of agentic AI-assisted engineering in regulated industries
coding.subtheme: Graduated human oversight tiers for agentic code generation
rq_alignment: human oversight and accountability in LLM systems
risk management and compliance in regulated contexts

synthesis.main_claim: The GAIE framework calibrates human oversight intensity to regulatory impact for agentic code generation through a three-tier model (OCM), preserving most agentic coding velocity while maintaining compliance evidence coverage.
synthesis.contribution: Introduces OCM as a deterministic decision function routing tasks by regulatory impact, customer proximity, reversibility, and data sensitivity; defines tier-specific evidence artifacts; maps against Bank of Thailand 2025 policy, MAS, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and EU AI Act.
synthesis.limitations: Provided text emphasizes framework design and analytical evaluation; no empirical deployment study or end-user conversational system evaluation is evidenced; conversational AI appears as evolutionary context rather than the paper's core governance object.
synthesis.use_in_review: Supporting evidence for graduated human oversight, compliance artifact design, audit trails, LLM safety controls, and cross-jurisdiction regulatory mapping in regulated agentic/LLM contexts; not central evidence for conversational AI governance per se.

evidence.claim: Paper presents GAIE as a three-tier graduated human oversight framework for agentic code generation in regulated domains
evidence.excerpt: We present the Governed AI-Assisted Engineering (GAIE) framework, a three-tier graduated human oversight model for agentic code generation in regulated domains.

evidence.claim: OCM classifies tasks by regulatory impact and routes them to oversight tiers
evidence.excerpt: GAIE introduces the Oversight Classification Model (OCM), a deterministic decision function that classifies code generation tasks by regulatory impact, customer proximity, reversibility, and data sensitivity

evidence.claim: Three oversight tiers include human-in-the-loop, human-over-the-loop, and automated-with-monitoring
evidence.excerpt: route them through one of three oversight tiers: human-in-the-loop (strategic functions), human-over-the- loop (customer-impacting), or automated-with-monitoring (inter- nal).

evidence.claim: Each tier requires evidence artifacts for compliance auditability
evidence.excerpt: Each tier defines required evidence artifacts for compliance auditability.

evidence.claim: Framework targets regulated industries including banking, insurance, healthcare, and energy
evidence.excerpt: Regulated industries — banking, insurance, healthcare, en- ergy — face supervisory expectations that extend to any AI system influencing decisions with customer or public impact.

evidence.claim: Governance challenge shifts to development pipeline when agents write regulated-function code
evidence.excerpt: When AI agents write code that governs regulated functions — credit approval logic, customer onboarding workflows, anti-money laundering screening rules — the oversight ques- tion transfers from model output governance to development pipeline governance.

evidence.claim: Evaluation uses regulatory coverage analysis, comparative framework analysis, and analytical productivity modeling
evidence.excerpt: Evaluation through regulatory coverage analysis, comparative framework analysis, and analytical pro- ductivity modeling suggests that graduated oversight preserves 84–97% of agentic coding velocity

evidence.claim: Conversational AI appears as an evolutionary phase of AI-assisted development, not the paper's main object
evidence.excerpt: Phase 2 — AI copilot (2023–2024). Conversational AI assistants integrated into IDEs generate multi-line code blocks in response to natural-language prompts.

evidence.claim: Reference architecture includes a human interaction layer and monitoring subsystem
evidence.excerpt: five subsystems: supervisor agent, collaborator agents, human interaction layer, evidence capture layer, and monitor- ing subsystem.

evidence.claim: Cross-cutting controls include LLM safety, sandboxing, and immutable audit trail
evidence.excerpt: Immutable audit trail. Complete provenance chain from task

evidence.claim: Prompt/response safety controls align with OWASP LLM Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS
evidence.excerpt: Prompt/response safety controls. Aligned with OWASP LLM Top 10 [36] and MITRE ATLAS [37]: prompt injection detection (LLM01)

evidence.claim: Authors disclaim that the work is thought leadership and not compliance advice
evidence.excerpt: This work constitutes academic thought leadership and does not constitute compli- ance advice or an institutional compliance assessment.
